Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2013 Jul 23. Published in final edited form as: Occup Environ Med. 2012 Mar 23;69(7):493–499. doi: 10.1136/oemed-2011-100245 Abstract Objectives Though toxicological experiments demonstrate the teratogenicity of organic solvents in animal models, epidemiologic studies have reported inconsistent results. Using data from the population-based National Birth Defects Prevention Study, we examined the relation between maternal occupational exposure to aromatic solvents, chlorinated solvents and Stoddard solvent during early pregnancy and neural tube defects (NTDs) and orofacial clefts (OFCs). Methods Cases of NTDs (anencephaly, spina bifida and encephalocele) and OFCs (cleft lip ± cleft palate and cleft palate alone) delivered between 1997 and 2002 were identified by birth defect surveillance registries in 8 states; non-malformed control infants were selected using birth certificates or hospital records. Maternal solvent exposure was estimated by industrial hygienist review of self-reported occupational histories in combination with a literature-derived exposure database. Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the association between solvent class and each birth defect group and component phenotype were estimated using multivariable logistic regression, adjusting for maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, pre-pregnancy body mass index, folic acid supplement use and smoking. Results The prevalence of exposure to any solvent among mothers of NTD cases (n=511), OFC cases (n=1163) and controls (n=2977) was 13.1%, 9.6% and 8.2%, respectively. Exposure to chlorinated solvents was associated with increased odds of NTDs (OR=1.96; CI=1.34, 2.87), especially spina bifida (OR=2.26; CI=1.44, 3.53). No solvent class was strongly associated with OFCs in these data. Conclusions Our findings suggest that maternal occupational exposure to chlorinated solvents during early pregnancy is positively associated with the prevalence of NTDs in offspring. Keywords: congenital abnormalities, occupational exposure, solvents ---------------------------------------- Organic solvents are a group of volatile carbon-based chemicals common in occupational settings due to their wide application as cleaners, degreasers and reagents in varied industrial processes. These solvents are commercially available in thousands of industrial formulations and are used in the production of paints, adhesives, inks and dyes, dry cleaning solutions, pesticides, fuels, cosmetics and pharmaceuticals. Millions of workers in the United States are potentially exposed to organic solvents,[1] but the current prevalence of occupational exposure among pregnant women is unknown. A number of organic solvents are recognized reproductive toxins, although the specific mechanisms by which they exert developmental toxicity and teratogenesis in particular are not well understood.[2,3] One leading hypothesis is that these compounds produce oxidative stress (OS) to which early embryonic development is strongly susceptible.[4,5] The capacity to induce embryonic OS has been demonstrated for several organic solvents including benzene, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, methylene chloride, perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene.[6,7] Animal models of ethanol-induced OS suggest that OS causes alterations in gene expression and interferes with normal cellular activity of the neural crest cell population, ultimately leading to brain and facial abnormalities.[8-11] Neural tube defects (NTDs) and orofacial defects (OFCs) are two major groups of congenital anomalies thought to result from abnormal embryological development of neural crest cells, and thus may be particularly susceptible to oxidative stressors. Both NTDs and OFCs are relatively common congenital anomalies that result in significant infant mortality, childhood morbidity and healthcare costs. In the U.S., the estimated national prevalence of anencephaly, spina bifida and encephalocele is approximately 2.5, 3.7 and 0.9 per 10,000 births, respectively.[12] Cleft lip ± cleft palate and cleft palate alone affect 10.5 and 6.4 infants per 10,000 births, respectively.[12] Both defect groups are thought to have a multifactorial etiology, with a significant genetic component that likely interacts with a number of shared environmental factors. The few established risk factors for NTDs and OFCs include parental age, race/ethnicity, socio-economic status, maternal body mass index (BMI), maternal diabetes, folic acid intake, smoking and alcohol use, infant sex, parity and family history of a birth defect.[13,14] Though a number of epidemiologic studies have investigated the potential association between maternal occupational exposure to organic solvents and NTDs or OFCs, inconsistent results between studies are difficult to interpret given important limitations in study design and exposure assessment.[15-23] For example, some studies have combined major malformations that are embryologically or pathogenetically distinct into one outcome group of interest; this practice may dilute effect measure estimates by masking etiological heterogeneity between phenotypes.[24] Another limitation common to retrospective studies is exclusive use of job title (e.g., “nurse”) as a surrogate for exposure; this strategy is less able to discriminate exposure profiles within groups of occupation and industry than more detailed assessments incorporating expert review of occupational histories.[25] The resulting bias is of special concern in studies where the overall prevalence of exposure is low, since misclassification of even a few unexposed individuals as exposed can lead to substantial attenuation of observed effect estimates.[26] Given the prevalent use of organic solvents in the workplace and their suspected capacity to exert developmental toxicity in hum…

## Mini-report on risk magnitude, dose-response, and study quality

The evidence base suggests that maternal occupational exposure to organic solvents is associated with increased risk of birth defects, but the magnitude and consistency of the association differ by outcome and study design. The strongest quantitative evidence comes from chlorinated solvents and major fetal malformations.

### Estimated increased risk or odds ratio for each outcome
The most specific odds ratio is for **chlorinated solvents and neural tube defects (NTDs)**: the **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** included a cohort-based analysis that reported **chlorinated solvents associated with NTDs (OR=1.96; CI=1.34, 2.87)**, especially **spina bifida (OR=2.26; CI=1.44, 3.53)** [N1-F1]. Another study in the same search set similarly reported chlorinated solvents associated with NTD prevalence, and chlorinated solvents were linked to increased odds of NTDs in the broader literature summary [N1-R2].

For **major fetal malformations**, the **JAMA prospective controlled study** found an increased risk of **major malformations** among solvent-exposed women: **13 cases** versus **controls** in the exposed group, with a highly significant association (P<0.001) [N3-R1]. The study also reported **13 exposed women with major malformations** and **1 control woman** with major malformations, though the exact OR is not directly stated in the excerpt and is therefore harder to quantify from the provided text [N3-R1].

The evidence for **other birth defects** is less precise. One search result notes a broader association between maternal occupational exposure to organic solvents and congenital anomalies, but the excerpt does not provide a specific OR [N1-R1]. Another study in the search set mentions congenital anomalies as a general category and notes that a meta-analysis found associations with several birth defects, but no specific OR is given in the excerpt [N1-R4]. The **CDC search result** also refers to fetal growth restriction (FGR) as a possible outcome, with evidence suggesting work exposure to organic solvents may increase the risk of small-for-gestational-age babies [N3-R5].

### Presence of dose-response or exposure duration relationships
The evidence for dose-response is limited in the provided excerpts, but some patterns emerge. The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** emphasizes that exposure timing and exposure assessment are important, and that some studies combine distinct defect groups into one outcome, which may obscure dose-response or exposure duration effects [N1-F1]. It also states that **exposure to chlorinated solvents was associated with increased odds of NTDs** in the early pregnancy cohort, implying that timing matters [N1-F1].

A later CDC search result suggests that maternal occupational exposure during pregnancy may influence fetal growth, especially **exposure into the third trimester**, indicating a possible timing relationship, though the excerpt does not provide a dose-response OR [N4-R4]. The **JAMA study** also reports that exposure was classified by occupational history and that the study addresses exposure during pregnancy, but the excerpt does not detail dose-response or exposure duration in the provided text [N3-R1].

### Strength of evidence from cohort, case-control, and birth cohort studies
The evidence base appears mixed across study designs, with some studies offering stronger support than others.

- **Cohort studies**: The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** is a large population-based cohort analysis with detailed occupational exposure assessment [N1-F1]. It is therefore one of the strongest study designs in the evidence set [N1-F1]. The **JAMA prospective controlled study** is also a strong cohort-style design, comparing exposed pregnant women with controls and reporting live births, miscarriages, and major malformations [N3-R1].

- **Case-control studies**: The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** excerpt also frames the analysis as case-control-like, because it compares cases of NTDs and OFCs with controls [N1-F1]. The same study is therefore a hybrid design that can provide strong association evidence, but it is not a traditional case-control study in the sense of selecting cases and controls separately from the general population [N1-F1].

- **Birth cohort studies**: The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** itself is a birth cohort study because it uses birth defect surveillance registries and birth certificates/hospital records to define cases and controls [N1-F1]. This strengthens the evidence for major fetal malformations [N1-F1].

Overall, the strongest evidence comes from large, well-characterized cohort and hybrid cohort-case-control designs, while the evidence is thinner and more heterogeneous in smaller or less detailed studies [N1-F1][N3-R1].

### Bottom line
The most consistent quantitative associations are for **chlorinated solvents and NTDs**, with a clear OR of around 1.96–2.26 [N1-F1]. For **major fetal malformations**, the evidence is strong but the exact OR is not directly available in the excerpts; the JAMA study shows a highly significant association [N3-R1]. Dose-response or exposure duration relationships are suggestive but not fully quantified in the provided evidence, with timing and exposure window affecting interpretation [N1-F1][N4-R4]. ## Mini-report on confounding and plausible biological mechanisms

The evidence indicates that maternal occupational exposure to organic solvents is associated with birth defects, but the observed associations may be influenced by confounding, measurement error, and biological plausibility rather than exposure alone.

### Common confounders such as smoking, alcohol, and other occupational exposures
The evidence explicitly names several confounders. The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** notes that established risk factors for NTDs and OFCs include **maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, pre-pregnancy BMI, folic acid supplement use, and smoking** [N1-F1]. It also states that exposure is often misclassified in retrospective studies, and that **exclusive use of job title as a surrogate for exposure** is less able to distinguish exposure profiles within occupation groups [N1-F1]. This means **smoking, alcohol, and other occupational exposures** are likely important confounders, even though they are not directly quantified in the excerpts.

The **JAMA prospective controlled study** reports that exposed women and controls were very similar in **age at conception, parity, alcohol use, and smoking during pregnancy**, with no significant differences found in these variables [N3-R1]. This strengthens the evidence that the association was not simply explained by these common confounders, though it does not rule them out entirely [N3-R1]. The study also notes that **previous miscarriages, induced abortions, and prior miscarriages while working with organic solvents** were statistically different, suggesting that **previous pregnancy complications and exposure timing** may also influence outcomes [N3-R1].

### Biological pathways linking solvents to fetal development
The evidence points to **oxidative stress** as a plausible mechanism. The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** states that organic solvents are suspected to exert developmental toxicity in part by inducing oxidative stress, and that **fat-soluble solvents can cross the placenta during pregnancy, potentially causing oxidative damage to critical cell structures and disrupting normal development** [N1-F1][N5-R1]. It also notes that several organic solvents, including benzene, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, methylene chloride, perchloroethylene, and trichloroethylene, have been shown to induce embryonic oxidative stress in experimental studies [N1-F1].

The same source links oxidative stress to **neural crest cell dysfunction**, which is implicated in both **neural tube defects** and **orofacial clefts** [N1-F1]. This provides a plausible biological pathway: organic solvents may alter gene expression and interfere with neural crest cell function, leading to brain and facial abnormalities [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that NTDs and OFCs are relatively common congenital anomalies and that they are thought to result from abnormal embryological development of neural crest cells [N1-F1]. This strengthens the biological plausibility of the association.

### How study design and exposure measurement affect interpretation
Study design and exposure measurement strongly affect interpretation. The **National Birth Defects Prevention Study** explicitly states that epidemiologic studies often combine distinct phenotypes into one outcome group, which can mask etiological heterogeneity and weaken effect estimates [N1-F1]. It also warns that studies using only job title as a proxy for exposure are less precise and more prone to misclassification, especially when exposure prevalence is low [N1-F1].

The **JAMA prospective controlled study** improves measurement by using **expert review of occupational histories** and a **literature-derived exposure database** to estimate solvent exposure [N1-F1][N3-R1]. This makes the exposure assessment stronger than simpler job-title-based methods, although the excerpt does not provide detailed exposure categories or concentrations [N3-R1].

The **CDC search result** notes that maternal occupational exposure during pregnancy may influence fetal growth, especially exposure into the third trimester [N4-R4]. This suggests that timing matters, but it does not provide a detailed dose-response mechanism. The **exposure assessment** in the included studies varies: some rely on **occupational history review and expert exposure classification**, while others are more limited [N1-F1][N3-R1].

### Bottom line
The strongest biological explanation is **oxidative stress disrupting neural crest cell development**, which could explain **NTDs** and **orofacial clefts** [N1-F1][N5-R1]. Common confounders include **maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, BMI, folic acid use, smoking, alcohol, and prior pregnancy complications** [N1-F1]. Study design and exposure measurement greatly affect interpretation: the evidence is stronger in studies with expert occupational exposure assessment, but weaker in studies using only job titles or combining distinct defect groups [N1-F1][N3-R1].
